content: 1. It is essential to identify which staff members would benefit most from reminders to ensure targeted and effective communication strategies. 2. Key messages for communication should be clearly defined and conveyed in simple, locally understandable language to maximize their impact. 3. The availability of appropriate expertise and resources to develop impactful communication materials must be assessed and ensured. 4. Staff members should be consulted to understand how they can contribute to communication exercises and to identify practices that would benefit from tailored reminders. 5. The objectives of a communication strategy to support surgical site infection (SSI) prevention at the local level must be clearly defined, and the strategy should be designed to cater to diverse audiences and media platforms. 6. A sample action plan, along with the identification of barriers and solutions for monitoring and feedback on infection prevention and control (IPC) practices, is provided in Part III of the WHO manual on improving IPC at healthcare facilities. 7. The interim practical manual supporting the implementation of WHO guidelines on core components of IPC programs can be easily adapted for SSI prevention programs. 8. In the SUSP project, local staff designed the content for reminders summarizing all SSI prevention measures. They categorized the measures into preoperative, perioperative, and intraoperative periods and preferred using the term wound infection instead of SSI. 9. The same content was adapted into various formats, such as posters, folded leaflets, and banners, to suit different audiences and purposes. 10. Clinical staff should be included in communication exercises to ensure that the language and format of materials are acceptable and effective. 11. All relevant staff disciplines should be engaged in reminders and communication plans to address SSI prevention risk factors effectively. 12. Communication strategies should involve all staff associated with surgery to ensure that the scientific content of messages aligns with care activities. 13. If certain SSI recommendations require communication to encourage implementation, all relevant staff groups should be involved in preparing and disseminating these messages. 14. Financial resources should be allocated to engage communication experts to work alongside local staff, if possible. 15. If adherence to a recommendation remains low despite communication efforts, hospital staff, including clinical, managerial, and communication experts, should review and adjust the strategy. 16. Communication materials and reminders should be consistent with training and education materials, and trainers should be involved in their development. 17. Senior management must visibly commit to supporting communication efforts as part of a multimodal strategy. 18. A dedicated and competent team should be identified to develop or support the creation of communication materials. 19. System changes may be necessary to ensure that promoted recommendations can be implemented effectively. 20. The institutional safety climate and culture should prioritize surgical safety issues and foster team cohesion and accountability among health workers. 21. Senior clinical leaders and managerial support are critical for successful implementation of SSI reduction programs. 22. Facilities should assess their safety culture and develop action plans for change, with clear timelines for review and follow-up. 23. Training opportunities should align with the desired cultural shift and be accessible to all staff. 24. Leadership communication has been shown to be effective in supporting infection prevention efforts. 25. Facilities should ensure that leadership is actively involved in addressing barriers to SSI reduction, including resource allocation. 26. Staff should feel safe raising concerns about patient safety and be involved in designing targeted interventions to improve surgical processes. 27. A culture of patient safety should be embedded in all aspects of SSI prevention, with achievements recognized and rewarded to sustain motivation and improvement. 28. Engaging patients in efforts to enhance the institutional safety climate can further support SSI prevention initiatives.
